title: registry-routing-compatibility-scoring-proposal
body:
Purpose:
This note proposes a lightweight, numerical compatibility scoring approach that the control plane can use to decide whether requests may be routed across model versions/variants and across regions. The goal is to make routing decisions deterministic, debuggable, and tunable so we can safely support version pinning, canary rollouts, multi-region fallback, and cost-aware routing without silent quality regressions.

Background and motivation:
- We regularly need to route requests between model variants: e.g., baseline v1 -> v2 canary, quantized fallback, or region-specific cheaper variants.
- Current heuristics are manual and binary (compatible / not compatible) and often lead to surprising behavior: cache misses, truncation regressions, or tokenizer mismatches.
- With Dedicated and Private deployments we must be strict about contractual pinning (customer-specified model version) while still supporting graceful degradation and automated routing for high availability.

Guiding principles:
1) Prefer explicit metadata over implicit assumptions. Each model artifact in the registry should publish the compatibility-relevant metadata used in scoring.
2) Make score and decision paths auditable — the control plane should log factors that caused an accept/reject or conversion path.
3) Allow configurable thresholds per customer/route (strict for pinned enterprise routes, permissive for host default).
4) Support runtime shims (e.g., tokenizer translation) when feasible and cost-effective, but prefer native compatibility.

Key definitions:
- Compatibility score (0-100): aggregated numeric score representing how safe it is to route a request from source variant A to target variant B.
- Native compatibility: no translation or state migration required. Score >= 85 by default.
- Transformable compatibility: requires a cheap runtime shim (tokenizer mapping, prefix normalization). Score between 60-84.
- Incompatible: requires model transformation or retraining, or would break user-visible behavior. Score < 60.

Metadata fields required on registry entries (minimum):
- model_id (string), version (semver-like), architecture (gpt-2/3/llama/graph...), tokenizer_hash (sha256), vocab_size (int), embedding_dim (int), quant_profile (fp16/int8/llm-int8...), supported_kernels (comma list), seq_len_95p (int), prefix_cache_schema_hash (sha256 or empty), stateful_cache_required (bool), pooling/attention-alg flags, regional_constraints (list), lineage_base_model (if fine-tuned).
- Example metadata snippet (text):
  model_id: "redwood/rdw-gpt-10b"
  version: "2025.01.12"
  architecture: "transformer-decoder"
  tokenizer_hash: "b3f7..."
  quant_profile: "int8-approx"

Compatibility scoring components and weights (proposal):
- Tokenizer compatibility (30 pts): exact tokenizer_hash match -> 30. Same vocab_size and deterministic mapping (with simple extra tokens) -> 20. Different tokenizer family -> 0.
- API/IO contract (20 pts): identical generation APIs (stop tokens, sampling behavior, logits shaping) -> 20. Minor mismatch (nucleus vs top-k defaults) -> 10. Major mismatch -> 0.
- KV/prefix cache schema (15 pts): same schema/hash -> 15, compatible schema with shim -> 8, incompatible (state required but missing) -> 0.
- Quantization/kernel compatibility (15 pts): supported_kernels intersection sufficient for target hardware -> 15. Missing kernels but software fallback available -> 8. No fallback -> 0.
- Seq length and performance envelope (10 pts): target seq_len_95p >= request expected length -> 10. Otherwise -> floor proportional score.
- Regional/deployment constraints (10 pts): region available & allowed by policy -> 10. Otherwise -> 0.

Score aggregation: simple additive sum (0-100). Default thresholds: >=85 native route; 65-84 allow with shim/transform; 40-64 route with degradation + explicit audit/log; <40 disallow route and fall back to a compatible variant or incumbent SLA route.

Routing policy precedence (control-plane decision order):
1) Explicit customer pin: If a customer pins a model version, enforce routing to pinned variant if available in-region/cluster. If not available, check compatibility score to decide whether to route to a compatible variant or fail.
2) Canary and rollout rules: weight-based canaries only target models with score >= 75 unless an explicit conversion shim is configured.
3) Region preference: prefer same-region replicas of the model; if unavailable, consider cross-region only if score >= 80 and latency SLO still met.
4) Cost-aware fallback: prefer cheaper variant (quantized) only when score >= 70 and regression budget allows.
5) Capacity/backpressure: if preferred variant is overloaded, route to next-highest score variant that meets latency/cost constraints.

Decision logging: each control-plane routing decision must emit a JSON-visible audit object including: source_model, target_model, compatibility_score, contributing_factors (list), selected_policy (which precedence rule triggered), latency_estimate, and action_taken (route/shim/fail).

Example compatibility cases (text table):
- Case A: rdw-gpt-10b v2025.01.12 -> rdw-gpt-10b-quant-int8 v2025.02.01
  tokenizer: same (30) | api: identical (20) | kv-cache: same (15) | kernels: software fallback present (8) | seq_len: same (10) | region: allowed (10) => score 93 (native-ish; allowed)
- Case B: rdw-chat-3 v1 -> rdw-chat-3-finetune-safety v1.2
  tokenizer: same (30) | api: minor sampling delta (10) | kv-cache: same (15) | kernels: full match (15) | seq_len: same (10) | region: allowed (10) => score 90 (allowed)
- Case C: base-model-3 v1 -> finetune-with-different-tokenizer v2
  tokenizer: mismatch (0) | api: same (20) | kv-cache: incompatible (0) | kernels: match (15) | seq_len: smaller (5) | region: allowed (10) => score 50 (transform required; likely reject for strict pinned routes)

Multi-region considerations and control plane reconciliation:
- Registry metadata is authoritative in the global control plane. Each region maintains a read-only cache plus a lightweight diff/subscribe feed for updates.
- For routing decisions we require a region-level strong-read of the local model availability and compatibility cache; if the region cache is stale, the control plane should prefer safe defaults (reject cross-region routing when pinned).
- To support low-latency failover, regions should pre-compute compatibility scores for top N likely cross-region mappings (based on historical traffic patterns) and keep them refreshed asynchronously.
- Replica creation workflow: when a model is replicated to a region, the replication job must validate the local hardware/kernels and produce a region-specific compatibility delta (e.g., missing kernel -8). This delta is applied to global score to produce region score.

Pinning workflows and failure modes:
- Customer pin present and target unavailable in-region:
  - If region_score >= pin_threshold (default 85) -> route.
  - Else if region_score >= fallback_threshold (default 65) and customer allowed auto-fallback -> route with explicit warning and telemetry.
  - Else -> fail the request and return a clear error code indicating pinned model not available (error doc includes reconciliation steps).
- Rollback: if a rollout increases error rates or decreases quality, the control plane should revert traffic to last-known-good variant. We require that the last-known-good variant is stored with its score and a snapshot of contributing factors so rollback is deterministic.

Telemetry and SLOs to monitor:
- Per-route compatibility score histogram.
- Count of shim-based conversions performed and mean added latency.
- Pinned-route failures due to unavailable region variants.
- Quality regressions post-routing (tie to eval harness and prompt set).
- Cross-region routing latency percentiles and error rates.

Operational safety knobs (configurable):
- Per-customer pin_strictness: strict|permissive|allow_shim.
- Score thresholds overrides per route.
- Blacklist of variants that must never be used as fallback for legal/compliance reasons.

Implementation notes (control-plane):
- Add a CompatibilityService that computes and caches pairwise compatibility scores. Expose API: getScore(source_model, target_model, region). Implement incremental recompute on metadata changes.
- Hook the routing decision in RouterService to call CompatibilityService with short-circuiting for pinned models.
- Emit provenance events into the event log for auditability.
- Provide admin UI in Console showing per-model pair scores and the contributing metadata diffs.

Open questions / trade-offs:
1) How much weight to give tokenizer mismatches vs KV-cache mismatches? (tokenizer mismatches can be catastrophic for chat flows).
2) Should we permit automatic tokenizer translation shims for enterprise customers? This opens up fidelity issues.
3) How to score behavioral changes that are not visible in metadata (e.g., different pretraining distributions)? We may need eval-harness-based adjustments to the compatibility score.
4) Volume of pairwise scores could be O(N^2). We need a pruning strategy (cache only top-k relevant pairs per model).

Next steps / proposed roadmap:
- (2w) Finalize metadata schema and implement tokenizer_hash & prefix_cache_schema_hash fields in registry ingestion.
- (4w) Implement CompatibilityService MVP that computes scores using the weights above and stores top-100 pairs per model.
- (6w) Integrate into RouterService for pinned-route checks and add telemetry hooks.
- (8-12w) Console visualization and per-customer threshold overrides.

Appendix: quick heuristics for triage (notes to on-call):
- If users report truncation or garbled output after a rollout -> check tokenizer_hash delta first.
- If latency spikes after cross-region fallback -> check kernel availability and seq_len percentiles.
- For customer pin errors -> always surface the exact compatibility score and the highest negative contributing factor in the error message for troubleshooting.

Contact and authors: Asha Patel (author), collaborators Marcus Lee, Rita Gomez, Evan Cho.

This doc is intentionally prescriptive but lightweight — aim is to land an MVP that reduces silent regressions and makes routing decisions auditable and tuneable.
